_link.title: I can define and identify peak voltage (Vp) on an EMF-time graph

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best defines the peak voltage of an AC waveform?
toLevel2.correct: The maximum voltage reached during one cycle of the AC signal
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Peak voltage (Vp) is the amplitude of the sine wave — the highest voltage above the zero line in one complete cycle.

distractors.answer: The average voltage over one complete cycle
distractors.explanation: The average voltage of a full AC cycle is zero. Peak voltage is the maximum value.

distractors.answer: The difference between the highest and lowest voltages
distractors.explanation: This describes the peak-to-peak voltage, which is 2Vp, not the peak voltage itself.

distractors.answer: The voltage at the midpoint of the waveform
distractors.explanation: The midpoint of the AC waveform is zero volts. Peak voltage is the maximum value.

toLevel2.question: On a voltage-time graph of an AC signal, the peak voltage can be identified as which one of the following?
toLevel2.correct: The highest point above the zero line on the graph
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The peak voltage is the amplitude of the sine wave, read as the maximum positive value on the voltage axis.

distractors.answer: The point where the graph crosses the time axis
distractors.explanation: Where the graph crosses the time axis, the voltage is zero, not at its peak.

distractors.answer: The total height from the lowest point to the highest point
distractors.explanation: This describes the peak-to-peak voltage (2Vp), not the peak voltage.

distractors.answer: The value at the end of one complete cycle
distractors.explanation: At the end of one complete cycle, the voltage returns to the same value it started at, which may be zero.

toLevel2.question: An AC voltage signal has a peak voltage of 100 V. Which one of the following is closest to the peak-to-peak voltage?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The peak-to-peak voltage is twice the peak voltage: Vp-p = 2 × Vp = 2 × 100 = 200 V.

distractors.explanation: 100 V is the peak voltage, not the peak-to-peak voltage.
This is Vp × √2, which is not how peak-to-peak voltage is calculated.
The peak-to-peak voltage is 2 × Vp = 200 V, not Vp/2.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following correctly identifies the symbol for peak voltage?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Peak voltage is denoted Vp, where the subscript p stands for peak.

distractors.explanation: Vrms is the root-mean-square voltage, not the peak voltage.
Vp-p is the peak-to-peak voltage, which equals 2Vp.
Vavg is the average voltage. For a full AC cycle, this is zero.

toLevel2.question: An oscilloscope displays a sinusoidal AC waveform. The voltage axis shows the signal reaching a maximum of +340 V and a minimum of −340 V. Which one of the following is closest to the peak voltage?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The peak voltage is the maximum value above zero, which is 340 V.

distractors.explanation: 680 V is the peak-to-peak voltage (2 × 340 = 680 V), not the peak voltage.
240 V is approximately Vp/√2, which is the rms voltage, not the peak voltage.
170 V is Vp/2, not the peak voltage.

toLevel2.question: The peak voltage of an AC signal is always greater than or equal to its rms voltage.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Vp = Vrms × √2 ≈ 1.41 × Vrms. Since √2 > 1, Vp is always greater than Vrms.

distractors.explanation: Vp = Vrms × √2. Since √2 ≈ 1.41, the peak voltage is always about 41% greater than the rms voltage.

toLevel2.question: On a voltage-time graph, the peak voltage is measured from the positive peak to the negative peak of the waveform.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The measurement from positive peak to negative peak gives the peak-to-peak voltage (2Vp). Peak voltage is measured from the zero line to the positive peak.

distractors.explanation: The total distance from positive to negative peak is the peak-to-peak voltage. Peak voltage is from zero to the maximum.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about reading peak voltage from a graph.
toLevel2.sentence: The peak voltage is the {{blank:1}} value of the AC voltage on a voltage-time graph, measured from the {{blank:2}} line to the top of the wave.

1.correctExplanation: Peak voltage is the maximum (highest) voltage reached during the cycle.

distractors.explanation: The average voltage of a complete AC cycle is zero. Peak voltage is the maximum.
Minimum voltage is the most negative value. Peak voltage is the maximum positive value.

2.correctExplanation: Peak voltage is measured from the zero line (horizontal axis) to the highest point of the waveform.

distractors.explanation: Measuring from the negative peak gives the peak-to-peak voltage, not the peak voltage.
Peak voltage is not measured from the rms value. It is measured from the zero line.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about peak-to-peak voltage.
toLevel2.sentence: The peak-to-peak voltage is {{blank:1}} times the peak voltage. If Vp = 50 V, then Vp-p = {{blank:2}} V.

1.correctExplanation: Peak-to-peak voltage spans from the negative peak to the positive peak: Vp-p = 2 × Vp.

distractors.explanation: √2 relates peak and rms voltages, not peak and peak-to-peak.
The peak-to-peak voltage is larger than the peak voltage, not smaller.
71 V ≈ 50 × √2, which gives the rms-related value, not peak-to-peak.
25 V = Vp/2, which is not the peak-to-peak voltage.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about Australian mains electricity.
toLevel2.sentence: Australian mains electricity has an rms voltage of 230 V. The peak voltage is approximately {{blank:1}} V, and the voltage swings between +325 V and {{blank:2}} V each cycle.

distractors.explanation: 230 V is the rms voltage, not the peak voltage. Vp = 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V.
163 V ≈ 230/√2, which incorrectly divides by √2 instead of multiplying.

2.correctExplanation: The AC voltage swings symmetrically between +Vp and −Vp, so it reaches −325 V.

distractors.explanation: The voltage swings to −325 V, not just to zero. AC alternates between positive and negative peaks.
−230 V is the negative rms value, but the actual voltage swing reaches −Vp = −325 V.

toLevel3.question: An oscilloscope shows an AC waveform reaching +170 V and −170 V. Which one of the following is closest to the rms voltage of this signal?

distractors.explanation: 170 V is the peak voltage, not the rms voltage.
340 V is the peak-to-peak voltage (2 × 170), not the rms voltage.
85 V = Vp/2, which is not how rms voltage is calculated.

toLevel3.question: A voltage-time graph shows a sinusoidal waveform with the positive peak at +50 V. Which one of the following best describes the negative peak of this waveform?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A sinusoidal AC waveform is symmetrical about the zero line, so the negative peak has the same magnitude as the positive peak: −50 V.

distractors.explanation: The waveform does not only go to zero. It alternates symmetrically, reaching −50 V.
The negative peak has the same magnitude as the positive peak, not double.
The negative peak equals −Vp = −50 V, not −Vp/2.

toLevel3.question: James measures the peak-to-peak voltage of an AC signal as 400 V. Which one of the following is closest to the peak voltage?

distractors.explanation: 400 V is the peak-to-peak voltage. The peak voltage is half of this: 200 V.
283 V ≈ 400/√2, which confuses peak-to-peak with the rms conversion.
100 V = Vp-p/4, which is not how peak voltage is calculated.

toLevel3.question: Which one of the following best explains why the peak voltage is important in circuit design?
toLevel3.correct: Components must be rated to withstand the peak voltage, which is higher than the rms voltage
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The actual voltage reaches Vp = Vrms × √2 ≈ 1.41 × Vrms. Components must be rated to handle this maximum voltage to avoid damage.

distractors.answer: The peak voltage determines the average power delivered to a circuit
distractors.explanation: Average power depends on the rms voltage, not the peak voltage.

distractors.answer: Components only need to withstand the rms voltage, which is always higher than Vp
distractors.explanation: Vp is always higher than Vrms. Components must handle the peak voltage.

distractors.answer: Peak voltage is the only voltage that matters in AC circuits
distractors.explanation: Both peak and rms voltages are important. Rms voltage determines average power, while peak voltage determines maximum stress.

toLevel3.question: A function generator produces a 50 Hz AC signal with a peak voltage of 10 V. Which one of the following correctly describes one complete cycle of this waveform?
toLevel3.correct: The voltage rises from 0 to +10 V, returns to 0, drops to −10 V, and returns to 0 over 0.020 s
toLevel3.correctExplanation: One cycle of a 50 Hz signal takes T = 1/f = 1/50 = 0.020 s. The voltage follows a sinusoidal path between +Vp and −Vp.

distractors.answer: The voltage stays at +10 V for 0.020 s before dropping to −10 V
distractors.explanation: AC voltage varies continuously in a sinusoidal pattern. It does not stay at a constant value.

distractors.answer: The voltage rises from 0 to +10 V and stays there for one cycle
distractors.explanation: This describes a DC signal, not an AC signal. AC continuously alternates.

distractors.answer: The voltage rises from 0 to +10 V, returns to 0, drops to −10 V, and returns to 0 over 0.50 s
distractors.explanation: At 50 Hz, one cycle takes 0.020 s, not 0.50 s.

toLevel3.question: Two AC signals are displayed on the same oscilloscope. Signal A has a peak voltage of 20 V and Signal B has a peak voltage of 50 V. Which one of the following correctly compares the peak-to-peak voltages?
toLevel3.correct: Signal A: 40 V; Signal B: 100 V
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Vp-p = 2 × Vp. Signal A: 2 × 20 = 40 V. Signal B: 2 × 50 = 100 V.

distractors.answer: Signal A: 20 V; Signal B: 50 V
distractors.explanation: These are the peak voltages, not the peak-to-peak voltages.

distractors.answer: Signal A: 14 V; Signal B: 35 V
distractors.explanation: These are Vp/√2 (rms values), not peak-to-peak voltages.

distractors.answer: Signal A: 80 V; Signal B: 200 V
distractors.explanation: Peak-to-peak is 2 × Vp, not 4 × Vp.

toLevel3.question: The peak voltage of a sinusoidal AC waveform is always positive, even though the waveform itself goes negative.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Peak voltage (Vp) is defined as the maximum magnitude of the voltage — the amplitude — which is always stated as a positive value.

distractors.explanation: By convention, Vp is the positive amplitude. The waveform goes to −Vp, but the peak voltage value itself is positive.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about the relationship between peak and rms voltage.
toLevel3.sentence: The relationship between peak voltage and rms voltage is Vp = Vrms × {{blank:1}}. For Australian mains with Vrms = 230 V, Vp ≈ {{blank:2}} V.

distractors.explanation: The factor is √2 ≈ 1.414, not 2. Using 2 would give the peak-to-peak voltage from the rms.
1/√2 converts from peak to rms: Vrms = Vp/√2. The reverse gives Vp = Vrms × √2.
460 = 230 × 2, which would be the peak-to-peak voltage, not the peak voltage.
163 = 230/√2, which divides instead of multiplying by √2.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about reading an oscilloscope display.
toLevel3.sentence: If an oscilloscope shows a sinusoidal waveform reaching +60 V, the peak voltage is {{blank:1}} V and the peak-to-peak voltage is {{blank:2}} V.

1.correctExplanation: The peak voltage is the maximum positive value shown on the waveform, which is 60 V.

distractors.explanation: 120 V is the peak-to-peak voltage (2 × 60), not the peak voltage.
42 V ≈ 60/√2, which is the rms voltage, not the peak voltage.
60 V is the peak voltage, not the peak-to-peak voltage.
85 V ≈ 60 × √2, which is not how peak-to-peak is calculated.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about the AC waveform.
toLevel3.sentence: An AC waveform with a peak voltage of 325 V alternates between +325 V and {{blank:1}} V. The voltage at the zero crossing points is {{blank:2}} V.

1.correctExplanation: A sinusoidal AC waveform is symmetrical, alternating between +Vp and −Vp.

distractors.explanation: The waveform reaches −325 V, not just zero.
The negative peak equals −Vp = −325 V, not −2Vp.

2.correctExplanation: At the zero crossing points, the voltage passes through zero as it transitions between positive and negative halves.

distractors.explanation: 325 V is the peak voltage. At zero crossings, the voltage is zero.
230 V is the rms voltage. At zero crossings, the instantaneous voltage is zero.

toLevel4.question: An oscilloscope displays an AC signal with divisions set to 50 V per division. The waveform extends 3 divisions above the zero line and 3 divisions below it. Which one of the following is closest to the peak voltage?

distractors.explanation: 300 V is the peak-to-peak voltage (6 divisions × 50 V/division), not the peak voltage.
This is Vp/√2, the rms voltage, not the peak voltage.
50 V is one division. The waveform extends 3 divisions, giving Vp = 150 V.

toLevel4.question: A power supply is rated at 12 V rms. Which one of the following is closest to the peak voltage that components in the circuit must withstand?

distractors.explanation: 12 V is the rms voltage. The actual peak voltage is higher: 12 × √2 ≈ 17 V.
24 V = 2 × 12, which is not how peak voltage is calculated from rms.
8.5 V = 12/√2, which converts the wrong way.

toLevel4.question: A laboratory signal generator produces a 50 Hz sinusoidal signal. The peak-to-peak voltage is measured as 28 V. Which one of the following is closest to the rms voltage?

distractors.explanation: 14 V is the peak voltage. The rms voltage is Vp/√2 ≈ 9.9 V.
28 V is the peak-to-peak voltage, not the rms voltage.
This does not follow from the correct conversion from peak-to-peak to rms voltage.

toLevel4.question: Liam reads an oscilloscope and reports the peak-to-peak voltage as 200 V. He then calculates the rms voltage as 200/√2 = 141 V. Which one of the following best evaluates his calculation?
toLevel4.correct: Liam is incorrect; he should first halve the peak-to-peak voltage to get Vp = 100 V, then divide by √2 to get Vrms ≈ 71 V
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Vp = Vp-p/2 = 100 V. Vrms = 100/√2 ≈ 71 V. Liam divided the peak-to-peak voltage by √2 instead of first finding Vp.

distractors.answer: Liam is correct; dividing peak-to-peak by √2 gives the rms voltage
distractors.explanation: The rms conversion factor applies to the peak voltage, not the peak-to-peak voltage. Liam should first halve.

distractors.answer: Liam is incorrect; the rms voltage is always equal to the peak-to-peak voltage
distractors.explanation: The rms voltage is always less than both the peak and peak-to-peak voltages.

distractors.answer: Liam is incorrect; he should multiply the peak-to-peak voltage by √2
distractors.explanation: Multiplying by √2 would give a larger value. The correct process is to halve first, then divide by √2.

toLevel4.question: A transformer secondary coil produces an rms voltage of 50 V. An oscilloscope is connected to the output. Which one of the following is closest to the peak voltage displayed on the oscilloscope?

distractors.explanation: 50 V is the rms voltage. The oscilloscope displays the instantaneous voltage, which peaks at 71 V.
100 V = 2 × 50, which is not how peak voltage is calculated from rms.
35 V = 50/√2, which converts the wrong way.

toLevel4.question: An AC generator produces a sinusoidal voltage with a period of 0.020 s and a peak voltage of 340 V. Which one of the following correctly gives both the frequency and the rms voltage?

distractors.explanation: 340 V is the peak voltage. The rms voltage is 340/√2 ≈ 240 V.
170 V = Vp/2, not Vp/√2. The correct rms voltage is 240 V.

toLevel4.question: An electrician measures the peak voltage of a household power point as 325 V using an oscilloscope. Which one of the following is closest to the rms voltage?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Vrms = Vp/√2 = 325/1.414 ≈ 230 V. This is the standard Australian mains rms voltage.

distractors.explanation: 325 V is the peak voltage, not the rms voltage.
650 V is the peak-to-peak voltage (2 × 325), not the rms voltage.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about an oscilloscope reading.
toLevel4.sentence: An oscilloscope set to 100 V/div shows an AC waveform reaching 2.5 divisions above zero. The peak voltage is {{blank:1}} V and the rms voltage is approximately {{blank:2}} V.

distractors.explanation: 500 V would be the peak-to-peak voltage (5 divisions × 100 V), not the peak voltage.
100 V is one division. The waveform extends 2.5 divisions, giving 250 V.
250 V is the peak voltage, not the rms voltage.
354 V = 250 × √2, which converts the wrong way.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about voltage conversions.
toLevel4.sentence: To convert from peak voltage to rms voltage, divide by {{blank:1}}. To convert from rms voltage to peak voltage, multiply by {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: Vrms = Vp/√2. Dividing the peak voltage by √2 gives the rms voltage.

distractors.explanation: Dividing by 2 gives half the peak voltage, not the rms voltage.
π is not involved in the peak-to-rms conversion for sinusoidal waveforms.

2.correctExplanation: Vp = Vrms × √2. Multiplying the rms voltage by √2 gives the peak voltage.

distractors.explanation: Multiplying by 2 gives the peak-to-peak voltage from the peak, not from rms.
Multiplying by 1/√2 would convert peak to rms, not the other way.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about a step-down transformer output.
toLevel4.sentence: A transformer outputs an rms voltage of 24 V. The peak voltage is Vp = 24 × √2 ≈ {{blank:1}} V and the peak-to-peak voltage is approximately {{blank:2}} V.

distractors.explanation: 48 = 24 × 2, which is not how peak voltage is calculated from rms.
17 = 24/√2, which converts the wrong way.
34 V is the peak voltage, not the peak-to-peak voltage.
96 = 24 × 4, which is not the correct calculation.

toLevel5.question: An AC signal has a peak voltage of 170 V at a frequency of 60 Hz. Which one of the following best describes the instantaneous voltage at t = T/4, where T is the period?
toLevel5.correct: The voltage is at its positive peak of +170 V
toLevel5.correctExplanation: For a sine wave starting at 0 V, at t = T/4 the wave reaches its positive peak: V = Vp × sin(2π × T/4 / T) = Vp × sin(π/2) = Vp = 170 V.

distractors.explanation: At t = T/4 for a sine wave starting at zero, the voltage is at its positive peak, not zero.

distractors.answer: The voltage is at its negative peak of −170 V
distractors.explanation: The negative peak occurs at t = 3T/4, not at t = T/4.

distractors.answer: The voltage is at the rms value of 120 V
distractors.explanation: The rms voltage is a time-averaged quantity. At t = T/4, the instantaneous voltage equals the peak voltage.

toLevel5.question: Two countries have different mains supplies. Country A has Vrms = 120 V at 60 Hz. Country B has Vrms = 230 V at 50 Hz. Which one of the following correctly compares their peak voltages?
toLevel5.correct: Country A: Vp ≈ 170 V; Country B: Vp ≈ 325 V
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Country A: 120 × √2 ≈ 170 V. Country B: 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V.

distractors.answer: Country A: Vp = 120 V; Country B: Vp = 230 V
distractors.explanation: These are the rms voltages. Peak voltages are higher by a factor of √2.

distractors.answer: Country A: Vp ≈ 240 V; Country B: Vp ≈ 460 V
distractors.explanation: These are 2 × Vrms (peak-to-peak from rms), not the peak voltages.

distractors.answer: Country A: Vp ≈ 85 V; Country B: Vp ≈ 163 V
distractors.explanation: These are Vrms/√2, which converts the wrong way.

toLevel5.question: A student observes an oscilloscope trace and incorrectly reads the peak-to-peak voltage as the peak voltage, reporting Vp = 400 V. The actual peak-to-peak voltage is 400 V. Which one of the following is closest to the correct rms voltage?

distractors.explanation: 283 V = 400/√2, which incorrectly uses the peak-to-peak value as the peak voltage.
200 V is the correct peak voltage, not the rms voltage.
400 V is the peak-to-peak voltage, not the rms voltage.

toLevel5.question: An oscilloscope displays two AC signals. Signal X has a peak voltage of 50 V at 50 Hz. Signal Y has a peak voltage of 50 V at 100 Hz. Which one of the following correctly compares these signals?
toLevel5.correct: Both have the same peak voltage and the same rms voltage, but Signal Y has twice the frequency
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Both Vp = 50 V, so both Vrms = 50/√2 ≈ 35 V. Frequency does not affect the peak or rms voltage.

distractors.answer: Signal Y has a higher rms voltage because its frequency is higher
distractors.explanation: Frequency does not affect rms voltage. Both signals have the same Vp and therefore the same Vrms.

distractors.answer: Signal Y has a higher peak voltage because it oscillates faster
distractors.explanation: Peak voltage is the amplitude, which is independent of frequency. Both have Vp = 50 V.

distractors.answer: Signal X has a higher peak-to-peak voltage because it has more time per cycle
distractors.explanation: Peak-to-peak voltage depends on amplitude, not frequency. Both have Vp-p = 100 V.

toLevel5.question: A capacitor in a power supply circuit is rated at 400 V. The supply is 230 V rms AC. Which one of the following best evaluates whether the capacitor rating is adequate?
toLevel5.correct: The rating is adequate because the peak voltage is approximately 325 V, which is below the 400 V rating
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Vp = 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V. Since 325 V < 400 V, the capacitor can safely handle the peak voltage.

distractors.answer: The rating is inadequate because 230 V rms is close to 400 V
distractors.explanation: The rms voltage is 230 V, well below 400 V. Even the peak voltage (325 V) is within the rating.

distractors.answer: The rating is inadequate because the peak-to-peak voltage is 650 V
distractors.explanation: Capacitors must withstand the peak voltage (325 V), not the peak-to-peak voltage.

distractors.answer: The rating cannot be evaluated without knowing the frequency
distractors.explanation: The frequency does not affect the peak voltage for a given rms voltage.

toLevel5.question: A technician measures the output of a generator using both a multimeter (which reads rms) and an oscilloscope. The multimeter reads 100 V and the oscilloscope shows a peak voltage of 141 V. Which one of the following best evaluates these readings?
toLevel5.correct: The readings are consistent because Vp = Vrms × √2 = 100 × 1.41 ≈ 141 V
toLevel5.correctExplanation: 100 × √2 = 141 V. The oscilloscope reading matches the expected peak voltage from the rms reading.

distractors.answer: The readings are inconsistent because the oscilloscope should show 100 V
distractors.explanation: The oscilloscope shows instantaneous values. The peak is Vrms × √2 = 141 V, not the rms value.

distractors.answer: The readings are inconsistent because the multimeter should read 141 V
distractors.explanation: The multimeter reads rms, which is Vp/√2 = 100 V. Both readings are correct.

distractors.answer: The readings are consistent because 100 + 41 = 141 V
distractors.explanation: The relationship is multiplicative (× √2), not additive.

toLevel5.question: A step-down transformer reduces 230 V rms to 12 V rms. An oscilloscope is connected to the secondary output. Which one of the following is closest to the peak-to-peak voltage displayed?

distractors.explanation: 12 V is the rms voltage. The peak-to-peak voltage is 2 × 12 × √2 ≈ 34 V.
24 V = 2 × 12, which incorrectly uses 2 × Vrms as peak-to-peak. The correct calculation uses √2 first.
17 V is the peak voltage (Vp = 12√2). The peak-to-peak voltage is double this: 34 V.

toLevel5.question: An engineer needs to select a diode that can withstand the peak inverse voltage of a 240 V rms supply. Which one of the following is the minimum peak voltage rating the diode must have?
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Vp = 240 × √2 = 240 × 1.414 ≈ 340 V. The diode must withstand at least this peak voltage.

distractors.explanation: 240 V is the rms voltage. The actual peak is 340 V, which the diode must withstand.
480 V = 2 × 240, which is not the peak voltage.
170 V = 240/√2, which converts the wrong way.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the sentence about comparing peak voltages of different mains supplies.
toLevel5.sentence: A country with 120 V rms mains has a peak voltage of approximately {{blank:1}} V. A country with 230 V rms mains has a peak voltage of approximately {{blank:2}} V.

distractors.explanation: 240 = 2 × 120, which is not how peak voltage is calculated.
85 = 120/√2, which converts the wrong way.
460 = 2 × 230, which gives peak-to-peak, not peak voltage.
163 = 230/√2, which converts the wrong way.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the sentence about oscilloscope readings and rms values.
toLevel5.sentence: A multimeter reads AC voltage as an {{blank:1}} value, while an oscilloscope displays the {{blank:2}} voltage waveform showing peak values directly.

1.correctExplanation: Standard AC multimeters are calibrated to display the rms (root-mean-square) voltage.

distractors.explanation: Multimeters display rms values, not peak values. Oscilloscopes show peak values.
While some meters use average-responding circuits, they are calibrated to display rms values.

2.correctExplanation: An oscilloscope displays the instantaneous voltage as it varies with time, showing the full waveform including peaks.

distractors.explanation: An oscilloscope shows instantaneous values, not rms. The rms value must be calculated from the peak.
The oscilloscope shows the complete instantaneous waveform, not just the average.
